warmup.q: Checkout writes balance = 70 to a replicated store and gets OK. 50 ms later a ledger service in another process reads the balance and gets the old value, 100. Which statement is true?
options: No replicated store may ever do this; the store is broken
The store isn't linearizable, but it could still be sequentially consistent
The store isn't even eventually consistent
warmup.why: Linearizability forbids it: the write finished before the read began, so real time puts the write first. Sequential consistency only needs one order that respects each process's own order, and putting the ledger's read before the write breaks nobody's order. Eventual consistency makes no promise about a single read, only that copies agree once writes stop. Serializability is about transactions, and it allows stale reads; this lesson shows a serializable database doing exactly this.

sections.h: A consistency model is a rule about which values a read may return
sections.html:
One copy of a balance has an obvious rule: a read returns the last value written. Make three copies and that rule stops being true, without anyone deciding to break it.

Take a store with a leader and two followers, as in the Replication track. Checkout writes balance = 70 for account acct-1001. The leader applies it at 10 ms. Follower f1 applies it at 15 ms, and follower f2, on a busy host, at 90 ms. A read at 20 ms returns 70 from the leader or f1 and the old 100 from f2. All three copies are healthy. They are just at different points in the same log.

Is the 100 a bug? That depends on what the store promised. A consistency model is that promise, written down: a rule that says which values a read may return, given the writes around it. It is a contract between the store and your code. A store with a strong model saves your code work; a weak one leaves the work to you.

To talk about models precisely, describe what the clients saw and nothing else. That description is a history. Each operation is a bar on a timeline: it starts when the request leaves the client and ends when the answer comes back. The store did the work at some instant inside the bar, and nobody outside the store knows exactly when. The figure shows a history with two bars.

Two orders are visible in any history. Real-time order: if one bar ends before another begins, every observer agrees the first came first. Program order: each client process runs one operation after another, so its own operations have an order too.

Here is the mental model for the whole lesson. Every model asks the same question: is there one order of these operations that a single copy could have produced, and that respects rule X? "A single copy could have produced it" means each read returns the latest write before it in that order. Only rule X changes. Linearizability's rule is real time. Sequential consistency's is each process's program order. Causal consistency keeps cause before effect and lets each process have its own order. The session guarantees only constrain your own session. Eventual consistency has no rule about reads at all.

In the figure, the write ended at 10 ms and the read began at 20 ms. In real-time order the read must say 70, so the history fails the strongest model. Put the read first and every process's own order still holds, so it passes the next one down. The lab builds a checker that asks this question for each model, and the demo below runs it.

The stale history passes as sequential because the checker found an order with ledger's read first. Each later history drops at least one more model, and eventual yes appears on every line: no finite history can break eventual consistency.

sections.h: Down the ladder: each model drops one demand
sections.html:
Start at the top. Linearizable means the store behaves as if there were one copy and each operation took effect at one instant inside its bar. Two consequences follow. A read that starts after a write has finished must see it. And once any read has returned the new value, every read that starts later must return it too, even while the write is still in flight. The next lesson is about linearizability alone.

Sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979) drops real time and keeps one order for everybody. Each process's operations must appear in the order that process ran them, and every process must agree on the same order. A read can be stale, as in the figure, but two clients can never see two writes in opposite orders. This is the frame "opposite orders" in the stepper below.

Causal consistency drops the single order. Each process may order concurrent writes its own way, but never an effect before its cause. "Cause" has a precise meaning: an operation causes everything later in its own process, and a write causes every read that returned its value, and those links chain. If the merchant read the question and then wrote the answer, the answer depends on the question, and nobody may see the answer and then miss the question. The Replication track's lesson on lag called this consistent prefix reads.

Below causal sit the session guarantees, promises to one client about its own session. Terry and colleagues named four of them in 1994. Read your writes: after you write, your reads see it. Monotonic reads: once you have seen a value, you never see an older one. Monotonic writes: your writes take effect in the order you made them. Writes follow reads: a write you make after reading something is ordered after what you read. You met the first two in the lag lesson, fixed with a session token that carries a log position.

Eventual consistency is the floor: if writes stop, all copies end up the same. It says nothing about what a read returns in the meantime. That makes it a liveness promise ("something good happens eventually"), and that is why every history in the stepper passes it.

Why accept anything below the top? Because strength costs availability, and Jepsen's map of models says exactly how much. When the network splits the replicas, nothing at or above sequential consistency can let every replica keep answering: some must refuse. Causal consistency and the session guarantees can be sticky available: a client that keeps talking to the same replica keeps working. Weaker models, such as read committed, can be totally available. So the question for each piece of data is: which is the weakest model my invariant tolerates?

try.title: Write a history that is causal but not sequential
steps: Open ModelsDemo.kt and find mine(). Replace its body with a history of your own: no process's bars may overlap, and each write to a key needs a new value.
Aim for causal yes and sequential no, without copying the "opposite orders" history. Hint: two processes are enough if each one also reads.
Run it with -Pargs=mine. If you get causal no, find the cause and effect you broke.
try.expect:
One answer: two regions each write the status and then read back the other region's value.

fun mine(): History = history {
    "eu".write("status", 2, 0..10)
    "eu".read("status", 3, 20..30)
    "us".write("status", 3, 0..10)
    "us".read("status", 2, 20..30)
}

mine
  eu        w(status,2)     0-10   r(status)=3    20-30
  us        w(status,3)     0-10   r(status)=2    20-30
  linearizable no  sequential no  causal yes  read-your-writes yes  monotonic-reads yes  eventual yes

In any single order one of the two writes comes last, and both reads after it would have to return that write. Each region on its own can put the other's write last, and no read depends on another, so causal holds. As shipped, mine() is the one-copy history and every model says yes.

sections.h: Serializable, linearizable and strict serializable answer different questions
sections.html:
Two words look alike and get mixed up in design reviews: serializable and linearizable. Both say "as if in some single order". They are about different things.

Serializability is about transactions, groups of reads and writes over many rows. The Transactions track defined it: the result is as if the transactions ran one at a time, in some order. Any order. Nothing says it must match the order in which they actually happened. So a serializable database may answer a read-only transaction from an old snapshot and still keep its promise, as long as the old snapshot is consistent.

Linearizability is about single operations on single objects, and it is all about recency: real time decides the order. It says nothing about a transaction that touches two rows. Two transfers that each check "total across both accounts at least 0" and then debit a different account can each run as linearizable single-key reads and writes and still drive the total negative. That is the write skew of the Transactions track's lesson on phantoms.

Put the two together and you get strict serializability: transactions in one serial order, and that order respects real time, so a transaction that starts after another committed sees its effects. Spanner sells this and calls it external consistency. FoundationDB offers it too. CockroachDB offers serializability with some recency guarantees, which falls short of strict. Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, which allows write skew, so it doesn't reach the serializable rung at all.

The gap between serializable and strict serializable is easy to fall into with replicas. Picture a ledger database that runs every write transaction on the leader, one at a time, so it is serializable by construction. To take load off the leader, read-only transactions run on a follower that applies commits 50 ms late. Checkout commits a payment at 30 ms. A ledger report at 60 ms reads the follower and sees neither the new balance nor the payment row. Both are missing together, so the snapshot is consistent and the history is serializable: put the report before the payment. It is not strict serializable, because the payment committed before the report began.

For your designs, ask two separate questions. Does this invariant span several rows (needs serializable transactions)? Does any reader learn about a write through another channel and then expect to see it (needs linearizability, or strict serializability for multi-row reads)?

try.title: A serializable database that returns stale data
steps: Run SnapshotDemo: the leader runs write transactions one at a time; read-only transactions run on a consistent snapshot, first on a follower 50 ms behind, then on the leader.
Before you run it, predict what T3 reads in each setup, and which setup is strict serializable.
Then run it with -Pargs=5 to put the follower only 5 ms behind. Does that make it strict serializable, or just less likely to show?

code.title: in the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.cons.l01.demo.SnapshotDemoKt -q ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.cons.l01.demo.SnapshotDemoKt -Pargs=5 -q

try.expect:
read-only transactions on a follower (50 ms behind)
  T1 setup       0-5    writes balance=100
  T2 checkout   20-30   writes balance=70, pay-7=captured
  T3 ledger     60-70   reads  balance=100, pay-7=-
  T4 ledger    100-110  reads  balance=70, pay-7=captured
  serializable: yes, as T1, T3, T2, T4
  strict serializable (the order must also respect real time): no
  key balance on its own: linearizable no, sequential yes

read-only transactions on the leader
  T1 setup       0-5    writes balance=100
  T2 checkout   20-30   writes balance=70, pay-7=captured
  T3 ledger     60-70   reads  balance=70, pay-7=captured
  T4 ledger    100-110  reads  balance=70, pay-7=captured
  serializable: yes, as T1, T2, T3, T4
  strict serializable (the order must also respect real time): yes
  key balance on its own: linearizable yes, sequential yes

On the follower, T3 sees the balance and the payment both missing: consistent, serializable as T1, T3, T2, T4, and stale. On the leader, the same transactions are strict serializable. With a 5 ms lag T3 happens to see everything, so this run is strict serializable too; a T3 that starts 2 ms after T2's commit would still miss it. A smaller lag shrinks the window and leaves the guarantee unchanged.

sections.h: CAP, as Brewer said it and as Gilbert and Lynch proved it
sections.html:
Eric Brewer put CAP forward in a keynote at the PODC conference in 2000, as a conjecture: a shared-data system can have at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance. He gave no precise definitions. The slogan "pick two of three" grew out of that talk, and it is wrong in a way worth understanding.

In 2002 Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch turned the conjecture into a theorem by pinning down each word. Consistency means linearizability of one read/write register. Availability means every request that reaches a node that hasn't failed gets a non-error answer. A partition means the network may lose any number of messages between nodes. The theorem: in an asynchronous network (one with no upper bound on how long a message may take), no system can guarantee both consistency and availability while messages can be lost.

The proof fits in a paragraph. Put one replica in the EU and one in the US, and cut the link between them. A payment arrives in the EU and debits the balance. A read arrives in the US. Availability says the US replica must answer. It has heard nothing from the EU, so it answers with the old balance. The write had finished before the read began, so linearizability is broken. To stay linearizable, the US replica must refuse or wait until the link returns, and then it isn't available.

Now what the theorem doesn't say. It doesn't let you "pick" partition tolerance away: networks lose messages whether you choose it or not (the Faults, time and truth track opened with that). The honest reading is "when a partition happens, a system either stays linearizable or keeps every replica answering". It says nothing about the long stretches with no partition, nothing about latency, and nothing about models other than linearizability or faults other than lost messages. Its availability is extreme: one refusing replica breaks it. Martin Kleppmann points out that a single-leader database with asynchronous followers is neither CAP-consistent (follower reads are stale) nor CAP-available (a client cut off from the leader can't write), and is still a perfectly useful system. Labels like "CP" and "AP" hide more than they tell.

Brewer himself revisited it in 2012: partitions are rare, so a design should detect one, enter an explicit partition mode that limits what is allowed, and reconcile afterwards. His example is an ATM that keeps paying out while cut off, but only up to a small limit, and settles the difference later. A card issuer's stand-in processing, which approves small authorizations when the issuer can't be reached, makes the same trade.

try.title: Answer or refuse during a partition
steps: Run CapDemo. Three replicas of one balance (eu, us, apac); from 1,000 ms to 3,000 ms eu is cut off from both others. The same requests run twice: once where every replica answers from its own copy, once where a request needs a majority of 2 of 3.
Before you run it, predict what checkout's write at 1,100 ms gets in each mode, and what ledger's read at 1,200 ms returns.
Look at the latencies before the partition too. Which mode pays on a healthy day?
try.expect:
available: every replica answers from its own copy
      0 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=70  ok    after 1 ms
    100 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 1 ms
   1000 ms  eu is cut off from us and apac
   1100 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=40  ok    after 1 ms
   1200 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 1 ms
   1300 ms  apac  fraud     writes balance=55  ok    after 1 ms
   3000 ms  the network heals
   3500 ms  eu    checkout  reads  balance     55    after 1 ms
   3500 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     55    after 1 ms
  the history of answered requests: linearizable no, eventual yes

consistent: a request must reach a majority (2 of 3 replicas) first
      0 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=70  ok    after 81 ms (via us)
    100 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 81 ms (via eu)
   1000 ms  eu is cut off from us and apac
   1100 ms  eu    checkout  writes balance=40  refused after 500 ms: can't reach a majority
   1200 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     70    after 121 ms (via apac)
   1300 ms  apac  fraud     writes balance=55  ok    after 121 ms (via us)
   3000 ms  the network heals
   3500 ms  eu    checkout  reads  balance     55    after 81 ms (via us)
   3500 ms  us    ledger    reads  balance     55    after 81 ms (via eu)
  the history of answered requests: linearizable yes, eventual yes

In available mode eu accepts the 40 and us goes on saying 70: every replica answered and the history isn't linearizable. Last write wins then picks apac's 55, so checkout's 40 vanished without an error. In consistent mode eu refuses for the whole partition while us and apac carry on, and the history is linearizable. Notice the healthy-day cost: 81 ms instead of 1 ms for every request, because each one waits for a round trip to a second replica. CAP doesn't mention it; the next section does.

refs.title: Brewer, CAP Twelve Years Later: How the Rules Have Changed (InfoQ)
Kleppmann, Please stop calling databases CP or AP

sections.h: PACELC, and the knobs that pick a model per request
sections.html:
The CAP demo's consistent mode paid 80 ms on every request with no partition anywhere. That cost is with you every day, and Daniel Abadi's PACELC (2012, say "pass-elk") names it: if there is a partition (P), choose availability (A) or consistency (C); else (E), choose latency (L) or consistency (C). A replicated store that waits for other replicas before answering is consistent and slow; one that answers from the nearest copy is fast and stale. Inside one data centre the wait is a millisecond or two; between regions it is a round trip of tens of milliseconds, about 70 ms between the US east coast and Europe.

Abadi labelled systems by their defaults: Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak as PA/EL, BigTable and HBase as PC/EC, and the MongoDB of 2012 as PA/EC. Treat those as descriptions of configurations, because every modern store lets you pick per request. The table maps the settings you are most likely to touch to the model each buys.

Store and setting What the setting controls What a client gets
Cassandra 5.0, ONE one replica must answer eventual; you can miss your own write
Cassandra 5.0, QUORUM writes and reads (RF 3) 2 of 3 replicas on each side, so they overlap every read meets every acknowledged write, but last-write-wins timestamps decide, and lesson 2 shows it still isn't linearizable
Cassandra 5.0, IF NOT EXISTS with SERIAL a Paxos round per partition linearizable compare-and-set on one partition
DynamoDB, default GetItem any replica answers eventual: may miss a write that just succeeded
DynamoDB, ConsistentRead=true the read reflects every write that succeeded before it up-to-date reads in one Region (twice the read cost; not on global secondary indexes)
MongoDB 9.0, default w: "majority", readConcern: "local" writes wait for a majority; reads take the node's newest data a read can return data that a failover later rolls back
MongoDB 9.0, readConcern: "majority" reads only what a majority has never rolled back, can be stale
MongoDB 9.0, readConcern: "linearizable" with w: "majority" the primary confirms it is still primary first linearizable for one document
MongoDB 9.0, causally consistent session, majority reads and writes the session carries its last seen cluster time causal, with the session guarantees
PostgreSQL 18, synchronous_commit = remote_apply commit waits until the synchronous standby has replayed it read-your-writes when you read that standby
Kafka 4.4, acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 how many replica copies hold a record before the producer hears OK durability for one partition's totally ordered log; consumers only see records that every up-to-date replica holds (the Messaging track has the mechanics)

Read the table as three questions you can ask of any store. How many copies must acknowledge a write before you hear OK? Which copy, or how many, may answer a read? Does the node answering a read check that it is still allowed to (still the leader, still holding the latest write)? Each extra "yes" moves you up the ladder and costs latency, which is PACELC's E. The Try-it times it on MongoDB.

Two traps. First, defaults are usually below linearizable: MongoDB's default read concern can return a write that a failover then rolls back, and DynamoDB's default read can miss a write that just succeeded. Second, a setting buys a model only for the operations that use it. A QUORUM write paired with a ONE read gives you ONE.

try.title: Time PACELC on a MongoDB replica set
steps: From the labs folder, start the three-member MongoDB 9.0 replica set: docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml up -d --wait (about 30 seconds, about 1.5 GB of Docker memory).

Run the commands below. First they time w: 1 against w: "majority" on a healthy set. Then db.fsyncLock() makes both secondaries stop applying writes, as if the primary were cut off from them, and the same write and three reads run with a 2-second limit.
Predict before you run: which write fails, and what do local, majority and linearizable reads return?
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: # a healthy set: time each write concern three times docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval ' db.balances.insertOne({_id: "acct-1001", balanceMinor: 10000}, {writeConcern: {w: "majority"}}); for (const w of [1, "majority", 1, "majority", 1, "majority"]) { const t = Date.now(); db.balances.updateOne({_id: "acct-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -100}}, {writeConcern: {w}}); print("w:" + w, Date.now() - t, "ms"); }' # both secondaries stop applying replication: the primary is as good as cut off for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncLock().ok'; done # the same write and three reads, each with a 2-second limit docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec mongo1 mongosh sfz --quiet --eval ' for (const w of [1, "majority"]) { const t = Date.now(); try { db.balances.updateOne({_id: "acct-1001"}, {$inc: {balanceMinor: -2500}}, {writeConcern: {w, wtimeout: 2000}}); print("w:" + w, "ok", Date.now() - t, "ms") } catch (e) { print("w:" + w, e.codeName, Date.now() - t, "ms") } } for (const level of ["local", "majority", "linearizable"]) { const t = Date.now(); try { const d = db.balances.find({_id: "acct-1001"}).readConcern(level).maxTimeMS(2000).next(); print(level, d.balanceMinor, Date.now() - t, "ms") } catch (e) { print(level, e.codeName, Date.now() - t, "ms") } }' for m in mongo2 mongo3; do docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml exec $m mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.fsyncUnlock().ok'; done docker compose -f env/mongo-rs.yml down -v

try.expect:
w:1 5 ms
w:majority 7 ms
w:1 3 ms
w:majority 4 ms
w:1 2 ms
w:majority 5 ms
1
1
w:1 ok 18 ms
w:majority WriteConcernTimeout 2018 ms
local 4400 4 ms
majority 9400 1 ms
linearizable MaxTimeMSExpired 2004 ms
1
1

On a healthy set, waiting for a majority cost 1 to 3 ms more than w: 1, here between containers on one laptop; between regions it would be a round trip. That is the E in PACELC. With the secondaries frozen, w: 1 still answered (available, and at risk of rollback) while w: "majority" gave up after 2 seconds: the P choice, made per write. The reads split the same way. local returned 4400, which includes two debits no secondary has; majority returned 9400, the last value a majority holds; linearizable refused, because the primary could not confirm with a majority that it was still primary. The timed-out write wasn't undone on the primary, which is why local shows it. Your timings will differ; compare the pairs.

refs.title: Abadi, Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (PDF)

analogy: A family shares one paper calendar on the fridge, and each person also keeps a pocket copy. The fridge is linearizable: whoever looks after a change was written sees it. Sequential is a rule that everyone copies changes in the same order, even if some copies are a day behind. Causal is weaker: if Dad moves the dentist because Mum's flight changed, nobody's copy may show the new dentist time without the new flight, but two unrelated changes can appear in either order. Read your writes is the rule that your own pocket copy always has what you wrote. Eventual is the promise that, if nobody changes anything for a week, all copies will match. The analogy breaks on cost: copying a calendar is free, while every rung up the ladder makes each real request wait for more machines to agree.
world: Your payment flows lean on these models whether or not anyone wrote them down. An authorization service that writes to Oracle and immediately reads back through a read replica needs read-your-writes, and gets it only if the read goes to the primary or carries a position, as the Replication track's lag lesson showed. A Kafka consumer that receives payment-captured and then looks the payment up in a database is relying on the database being linearizable with respect to the producer's write; the Kafka message is a second channel that carries timing. A Temporal workflow that records an activity result and then branches on it relies on Temporal's own history store being consistent, which it is for one workflow. When you pick DynamoDB's default read for a balance check, or MongoDB's local read for a refund decision, you have picked eventual consistency for that decision. Write the model next to each read path in the design doc, and the weakest acceptable one for each invariant.
mistake: Treating "strongly consistent" in a product page as a single, known guarantee. People read it, assume it means linearizable for every operation, and design a uniqueness check or a cross-service handshake on top. Then they find that the guarantee covered only some reads (DynamoDB's strongly consistent reads skip global secondary indexes), only some settings (MongoDB's linearizable read needs w: "majority" and a single-document filter), or only a single key. The mistake happens because the phrase is vague, and every vendor uses it. The fix: name the model, the operations and the settings in your design ("linearizable single-document reads with readConcern: linearizable and w: majority"), and test the claim with a history checker like the one in this lesson's lab before you rely on it.

compare.title: The same balance read, two promises

a.label: MongoDB, default
a.title: fast, may be rolled back
a.html: val balances = db.getCollection("balances") // w: majority is the default since 5.0; reads use readConcern local val doc = balances.find(eq("_id", "acct-1001")).first() // newest data on the node you hit, including writes a failover can roll back

b.label: MongoDB, linearizable
b.title: slower, one document, primary only
b.html: val strict = db.getCollection("balances") .withReadPreference(ReadPreference.primary()) .withReadConcern(ReadConcern.LINEARIZABLE) .withWriteConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY) val doc = strict.find(eq("_id", "acct-1001")).maxTime(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS).first() // sees every majority write that finished before the read began

compare.note: The left read answers from whatever node it reaches with that node's newest data. The right read must go to the primary, and the primary confirms with a majority that it is still primary before answering, which costs a round trip and can block during an election, so set a time limit. It is linearizable only for a filter that matches one document.

worked.title: Name the model a payment read path really gets

steps.say: Start from the invariant, in words. Example: a refund may be issued only if the payment is captured and not already refunded. Two refund requests for one payment must not both pass.
steps.code:
invariant: at most one refund per captured payment
readers:   refund-service (decides), merchant dashboard (shows)
writers:   capture-service, refund-service

steps.say: Find the write setting. Here the refund is written to Cassandra 5.0 at QUORUM.
steps.code: val write = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "UPDATE payments SET status = 'refunded' WHERE payment_id = ?", paymentId) .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.QUORUM)

steps.say: Find the read setting and where it goes. The refund check reads at QUORUM too, so it overlaps every acknowledged write. That still allows two concurrent refund checks to both see captured and both write refunded: a check-then-act race, and no read model fixes that.
steps.code: val check = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "SELECT status FROM payments WHERE payment_id = ?", paymentId) .setConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.QUORUM)

steps.say: Pick the weakest model that keeps the invariant. "At most one" needs a linearizable compare-and-set on one row, which Cassandra offers as a lightweight transaction (Paxos, the subject of lesson 3). The dashboard can keep reading at ONE.
steps.code: val refund = SimpleStatement.newInstance( "UPDATE payments SET status = 'refunded' WHERE payment_id = ? IF status = 'captured'", paymentId) .setSerialConsistencyLevel(DefaultConsistencyLevel.SERIAL) val applied = session.execute(refund).wasApplied() // false: someone else refunded it first

steps.say: Write the result down next to the code, so the next person doesn't have to work it out again.
steps.code:
refund decision: linearizable CAS (LWT, SERIAL)   several round trips per write
refund display:  eventual (ONE)                   may lag by seconds

lab.title: A classifier for consistency models
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. They need no Docker and run in about a second. All 15 fail. Read History.kt first: Op, the history { } builder, and Search.legalOrder, which finds an order in which every read returns the latest write before it and which respects a mustPrecede relation you pass in.
Exercise 1: realTime(a, b) and programOrder(a, b). Each is one line.

Exercise 2: causalOrder(h). Start from program order, add an edge from each write to every read that returned its value (h.writeOf(read)), then close it under transitivity. A boolean matrix and a triple loop is plenty for histories this small.

Exercise 3: satisfies(h, model). Linearizable and sequential are one Search.exists over all ops each. Causal and the two session guarantees are one search per process, over all writes plus that process's own operations, each with its own relation. Eventual is true.

Run the tests until all pass. ModelsTest holds the stepper's histories; LadderPropertyTest checks 300 histories from a single atomic copy (every model must hold) and 300 random ones (a stronger model must always imply the weaker ones).
hints: Read your writes, per process p: a must precede b when both are p's, a is a write, b is a read and a came first. Monotonic reads: both are p's reads and a came first.

Causal per process: use the relation from causalOrder(h) unchanged. Edges that pass through other processes' reads are already in it, because you closed it over the whole history before restricting the search to one process's view.
If the property test fails, jqwik prints the seed and your assertion message includes the history. Paste it into a plain test with the history { } builder and print classify(h).

drill.title: Each model in one line
drill.prompt: Without looking, write satisfies(h, model) for all six models, given Search.exists(ops, mustPrecede), realTime, programOrder and causalOrder(h). For the per-process models, say which operations go into each search.

answer.html: fun satisfies(h: History, model: Model): Boolean { fun view(p: String) = h.ops.filter { it.kind == Kind.WRITE || it.process == p } return when (model) { Model.LINEARIZABLE -> Search.exists(h.ops, ::realTime) Model.SEQUENTIAL -> Search.exists(h.ops, ::programOrder) Model.CAUSAL -> causalOrder(h).let { before -> h.processes.all { Search.exists(view(it), before) } } Model.READ_YOUR_WRITES -> h.processes.all { p -> Search.exists(view(p)) { a, b -> a.process == p && b.process == p && a.kind == Kind.WRITE && b.kind == Kind.READ && programOrder(a, b) } } Model.MONOTONIC_READS -> h.processes.all { p -> Search.exists(view(p)) { a, b -> a.process == p && b.process == p && a.kind == Kind.READ && b.kind == Kind.READ && programOrder(a, b) } } Model.EVENTUAL -> true } }

recap: A consistency model is a rule about which values a read may return. Every model asks whether one order of the operations, one that a single copy could have produced, respects some rule; only the rule changes.

Linearizable respects real time; sequential respects each process's own order; causal keeps cause before effect per process; the session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads) constrain one session; eventual only promises convergence.
Nothing at or above sequential stays available on both sides of a partition. Causal and the session guarantees can be sticky available; weaker models can be totally available.

Serializable is about multi-row transactions in some order and allows stale reads; linearizable is about one object and recency and allows write skew; strict serializable (Spanner's external consistency) is both.
CAP, as Gilbert and Lynch proved it, covers one model (linearizability), one fault (lost messages) and an extreme availability. PACELC adds the cost you pay with no partition at all: latency.
Products let you choose per request: Cassandra levels, DynamoDB ConsistentRead, MongoDB write and read concerns, PostgreSQL synchronous_commit, Kafka acks. Defaults usually sit below linearizable.

explain.prompt: A product manager asks why the merchant dashboard sometimes shows a refund that the payments API says hasn't happened yet, when "the database is strongly consistent". Explain it in plain words.
explain.answer: The database keeps several copies, and each one learns about a change a few milliseconds apart. "Strongly consistent" in the vendor's docs only applies to certain kinds of reads with certain settings. The payments API reads with the setting that waits for the latest copy, so it sees exactly what has been committed. The dashboard reads with the fast default, which answers from whichever copy is nearest; right after a change, that copy may be ahead of or behind the one the API used. Here the dashboard's copy got the refund first, or the API was asked before the refund committed. Both answers are allowed by the promises we chose. If the dashboard must never contradict the API, it has to use the slower setting too, and every page load will wait a little longer for the copies to agree. For a dashboard a short disagreement is usually fine; for the refund decision itself, it is not, which is why that path uses the strict setting.

deeper.html:
Jepsen's map of consistency models puts the single-object models from this lesson and the transaction isolation levels from the Transactions track on one picture, joined at strict serializability, and colours each by how available it can be during a partition. It is the best one-page reference on the subject. The availability classes come from Bailis and colleagues' work on Highly Available Transactions, which showed that read committed, monotonic atomic view and the session guarantees need no coordination at all.

Viotti and Vukolic's survey defines more than 50 consistency notions precisely, for single objects without transactions, and orders them by strength. Their trick is to describe each model with two relations: visibility (which writes a read can see) and arbitration (one global order used to resolve conflicts). Linearizability, for example, is "one order that respects real time and from which every read's value follows".

The lab's checker treats each model as a search for an order, which is exponential in the worst case. Real tools avoid that for transactional histories: Jepsen's Elle infers the dependency edges between transactions from the values they read and looks for cycles, which is close to linear time. The next lesson builds the search for linearizability properly.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10 covers consistency models and CAP from the angle of replicated databases.
